playbook:
When an opponent publicly commits to a grim trigger ("the first time you defect, I defect every round after"), do not defect while more than one round remains — keep cooperating until the final round only, unless they break their promise first.

When there is exactly one round left, defect if it increases my chance to win (e.g., to break a tie or to take the lead). If defecting on the last round does not improve my standing, prefer cooperation only if that yields equal or better expected utility (rare).

When an opponent has cooperated consistently and given no credible reason to punish, keep cooperating through the penultimate round to maximize total payoff.

If an opponent has already punished me by switching to permanent defection (i.e., they actually defect following my defection), switch to permanent defection as well — do not attempt to resume cooperation unilaterally.

If an opponent announces a grim trigger and then indeed cooperates, treat the announcement as credible unless they deviate; do not test the grim trigger midgame because doing so burns future cooperative payoffs.

When facing tit-for-tat or similar conditional reciprocity, maintain cooperation except possibly defect in the very last round to exploit the one-shot advantage.

Do not defect midgame and then try to resume cooperation — grim-trigger-like strategies will permanently punish and yield a lower total payoff.

If the opponent’s strategy is unknown and multiple rounds remain, prefer initial cooperation to gather information; only consider midgame defection if I have strong evidence I can avoid permanent retaliation (rare and risky).

If the opponent claims a punitive rule but then violates it (e.g., they promised regretless cooperation but defected preemptively), treat them as untrustworthy and adopt a retaliatory/defection policy accordingly.

When choosing between maximizing round-by-round payoff and securing the match win, weigh remaining rounds and current score: favor mutual cooperation when future retaliation is possible and the match outcome is not determined; favor last-round defection only to change the final ranking.

When an opponent’s stated strategy is simple and consistent with observed actions (as in this episode), follow the cooperative-for-penultimate-rounds, last-round-exploit rule; revise only if observed behavior contradicts their statement.
